display_title: Good idea, interesting paper, but the experiment protocol could improve

content.title: Good idea, interesting paper, but the experiment protocol could improve
content.review:
### **Summary**:
 
This work proposes, perceptual DNNs, a new defense against adversarial attacks. The idea behind perceptual DNNs is to control the input to the network by letting the system to recreate (reconstruct) the input before feeding it to the classifier. The benefits of this concept are introduced via two implementations, one based on image inpainting, and a second one based on superresolution using a GAN. This approach can be combined with adversarial training, leading to additional robustness to both white-box and black-box attacks. The method achieves good results in CIFAR-10, SVHN, and Imagenette datasets, against FScattering and simple adversarial training.
 
---
 
### **Reasons for score**: 
 
I feel divided about this work in this current state, the reason why I am scoring it with a “**marginally above acceptance threshold**”, but I am trying to define it as “**borderline**”. The topic is clearly relevant, and the idea is well formulated, simple, and easy to reproduce. From the results, it seems to be effective, but I have concerns about the structure of section 4 and the experiments therein. I will elaborate on these concerns in the next sections.
 
---
### **Strengths**:
 
* I think the idea presented in this paper is interesting, and it is worth exploring.
* The proposed approach is quite generic and easy to reproduce.
* The proposed approach significantly outperforms the baselines in CIFAR-10, SVHN, and Imagenette.
* The paper is well written and to the point.
---

### **Weaknesses**:

I see some issues in the structure of section 4 and the decisions made to evaluate the approach:
* The experiment protocol is subsampling the test set. It seems that not all the images of the test set are used. Is this the case? If so, this makes a comparison with other approaches very complicated (for those papers coming after yours). I think the paper needs more clarity on this issue and probably a fix in order to keep experiment protocols as standard as possible.

* I think it would help to see the results in terms of model accuracy instead of attack accuracy. How much does the classification accuracy go down in each case? This can’t be perceived using the attack accuracy metric. In the end, what the approach is trying to achieve is to improve resilience to attacks to keep the classifier operative, working within a high-accuracy regimen, so it makes sense to evaluate based on the accuracy of the final task.

* I think Imagenette is typically intended to do quick testing. You already have results on CIFAR-10 and SVHN. I think the next logical step is to use ImageNet to test your approach, but I don’t see the need for Imagenette in this context. Presenting good results in ImageNet would make your “selling point” much stronger.

* I believe this paper may benefit from the following baseline: [Adversarial Robustness through Local Linearization](http://papers.neurips.cc/paper/9534-adversarial-robustness-through-local-linearization.pdf). It is one of the top approaches for adversarial defenses, along with FScattering. In fact, it is hard to tell which one produces the best results. I think it would be a good addition to the baselines.


---

### **Questions to be discussed during the rebuttal period**:

I would like the authors to discuss the concerns presented in the **Weaknesses section**.

---

### **Other considerations**:

None.

---

### **References**:

1. [Adversarial Robustness through Local Linearization](http://papers.neurips.cc/paper/9534-adversarial-robustness-through-local-linearization.pdf)
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for the constructive comments and time in reading and reviewing our paper. Please find the answers to your comments/questions below.

> The experiment protocol is subsampling the test set. It seems that not all the images of the test set are used. Is this the case? If so, this makes a comparison with other approaches very complicated (for those papers coming after yours). I think the paper needs more clarity on this issue and probably a fix in order to keep experiment protocols as standard as possible.

Thank you for pointing this out. We followed the advice and now all of the FGSM and PGD results on the updated article take all of the images into account. 
Regarding the 1px and 10px attacks, we estimated that this would take about 2 months, 1 month and a half and 4 months for respectively Imagenette, CIFAR and SVHN running in a RTX2080Ti. Therefore, it is not feasible currently.

> I think it would help to see the results in terms of model accuracy instead of attack accuracy. How much does the classification accuracy go down in each case? This can’t be perceived using the attack accuracy metric. In the end, what the approach is trying to achieve is to improve resilience to attacks to keep the classifier operative, working within a high-accuracy regimen, so it makes sense to evaluate based on the accuracy of the final task.

Following the advice, we changed the results from attack accuracy to classification accuracy for all of the tests.

> I think Imagenette is typically intended to do quick testing. You already have results on CIFAR-10 and SVHN. I think the next logical step is to use ImageNet to test your approach, but I don’t see the need for Imagenette in this context. Presenting good results in ImageNet would make your “selling point” much stronger.

Unfortunately, for ImageNet it would not be possible in the current time frame. Moreover, all of the methods use recent but not state-of-the-art inpainting and super-sampling methods. Therefore, they would have to be changed to state-of-the-art inpainting and super-sampling for results to really matter for ImageNet. 

Having said that, the results shown here already surpass the state-of-the-art in all problems and attacks tested. The adversarial trained NSR surpasses Fscattering in all cases and an adversarial trained FIR surpasses Fscattering in all but one case. Therefore, it would be reasonable to assume that with the performance of inpainting and super-sampling improving by using state-of-the-art methods, the method should perform even better in current and ImageNet datasets. 

> I believe this paper may benefit from the following baseline: Adversarial Robustness through Local Linearization. It is one of the top approaches for adversarial defenses, along with FScattering. In fact, it is hard to tell which one produces the best results. I think it would be a good addition to the baselines.

We followed closely the above baseline in the updated version. The method was also added in the Table.

display_title: Good results, while the big picture is unclear

content.title: Good results, while the big picture is unclear
content.review:
The author proposed a type of network architectures that are designed for better defenses against adversarial attacks, called $\varphi$DNN.
The idea is to insert a reconstruction layer to recover the corrupt input image as the new input image. They use super-resolution GANs and downscaling operations as one type of corruption/reconstruction, and auto-encoders for pinpointing input images with missing holes. These two techniques corresponds to two architecture augmentation, called FIR and NSR. They experimented on CIFAR/SVHN/ImageNet and show that such augmentation can improve the robustness of a deep classifier.

The positive factor is that the insertion of the corruption/reconstruction component indeed improves the robustness of a backbone network, as shown in Table 1. 

After reading this submission, this reviewer has several questions that remain unanswered.

1. The hypothesis is that humans are less prone to adversarial examples because humans have blind spots and can reconstruct the image. This leads to the design of input re-creation. However, a more reasonable explanation is that this input recreation can serve as a filter to ignore the adversarial perturbations. For example, the ablation methods in Table 2 can be considered as input corruption (no re-creation) and they can also improve the robustness, but the reason is not human eyes also do JPEG compression.
2. Human eyes may do input re-creation, but humans have no difficulties performing classification. But the test accuracies of NSR/FIR architectures are very low.
3. After adding the corruption/reconstruction component, the test accuracy becomes worse. If we simply prune a DNN, it will also be more robust to adversarial attacks, meanwhile achieving a lower test accuracy. Does this mean pruning DNNs is comparable to the proposed method?
4. Why view the input re-creation network and the task network as a whole? Similar to 1, these two parts can be completely decoupled and trained on different data distributions. Combining them all together and call them $\varphi$DNN seems a bit weird.
5. For NSR analysis, if we think from the perspective of robust training, it is natural to expect NSR outperforms SR. When we add noises, we essentially require the network to perform well in a small neighborhood, thus increasing the robustness.

Overall, while this paper provides good results (Table 1), this reviewer has doubts about the motivation and the hypothesis. In my view, input re-creation is the same as all other methods that try to filter adversarial signals, such as the methods in Table 2. Meanwhile, the results in Table 1 and Table 2 show that their method can achieve better robustness compared to commonly used baseline methods.

content.title: Clarifying the big picture
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for the constructive comments and time in reading and reviewing our paper.
Please find the answers to your comments/questions below.

1. Yes, there is both a bio-inspired motivation and a technical explanation for the results. The technical motivation was originally discussed in Section 3.1. There is a combination of factors here. As mentioned by the reviewer the filtering aspect is an important point. Moreover, there is (a) a timely varying corruption system which makes attacks non deterministic, (b) the decrease in the input distribution by adding noise which is also mentioned by the reviewer and (c) the real input to the system is mostly defined by the recreated input (which is a prediction of the system) and not by the dataset/input itself (this is the reason for super-resolution to be introduced after the denoising for example). The usual P(y|x) becomes P(y|z) in which z is the predicted input derived mostly from contextual hints. In fact, maybe the most profound point here is that the aim is in not relying on the input as much as possible. FIR output is basically 100% recreated and NSR has only a small fraction of the input being directly correlated with the output. 

2. For small images (CIFAR and SVHN) the proposed methods are slightly worse in accuracy in comparison with Fscattering (1.5 or 3% for FIR and 3 to 7% for NSR ). This is, however, false for large images such as the ones from Imagenette. In this case, the proposed method is even more accurate in NSR’s case (NSR is 4% more accurate) and performs similarly for FIR. We would like to mention that human eyes also perform relatively better than algorithms for larger images, so there is some resemblance there.

3.  Results with a pruned network were added to the updated paper. Its results demonstrate that pruned networks are not close in robustness to the current work. As the reviewer knows, DNNs trade robustness for accuracy so the drop in accuracy for robust classifiers is expected. This is shown in detail in the paper [“Robustness may be at odds with accuracy”].  Robust classifiers may never reach the accuracy of non-robust ones.

4.  In our opinion, the perceptual layer in \varphiDNN changes completely the nature of the system. Now, the input is not a creation of some external environment/dataset but mostly part of an internal recreation process. As correctly mentioned by the reviewer, they are decoupled for now. In our point of view, however, even if future developments connect both (e.g., with feedback signals), the main nature of the whole system barely changes.

5. Yes, we agree completely. We originally mentioned this point together with some other reasons for the robustness in Section 3.1. 

> Overall, while this paper provides good results (Table 1), this reviewer has doubts about the motivation and the hypothesis. In my view, input re-creation is the same as all other methods that try to filter adversarial signals, such as the methods in Table 2. Meanwhile, the results in Table 1 and Table 2 show that their method can achieve better robustness compared to commonly used baseline methods.

Usual pre-processing defenses are passive and strongly correlated with the input, i.e., they output f(x) and, consequently, the DNN outputs P(y|f(x)). Here, we are interested in P(y|z) in which z is a recreated image from a contextual hint. There is a weak correlation between x and z. In fact, z is strongly dependent on the prior learned by the predictor (in our case an inpainting or super-sampling neural network).

content.title: This paper proposes two approaches of input recreation (image inpainting and image super-resolution) to increase the robustness over adversarial attack.
content.review:
This paper presents leveraging two input recreation approaches, i.e., inpainting, and super-resolution, to enhance the model robustness against adversarial examples. Human perception systems inspire authors this idea, and they demonstrate its usefulness with a fair amount of experiments. However, the examplar content reconstruction methods are from previous works, and I feel questionable about the proposed input recreation methods' generability to real-world data. Meanwhile, there are several other content reconstruction approaches, like deblurring, denoising. Why only discuss SR and inpainting, and how do we know what kind of reconstruction approach is the best for a specific type of attack? 

In addition to the choice of content reconstruction, I feel doubtful about your experimental setting. For instance, the training data for image super-resolution obtained by adding noise and bi-linear downsampling is trivial. Doing such ways will bias your reconstruction model to this simple type of degradation. Thus, I am afraid that feeding other types of data will make your model work or not, like different noise distribution or different levels of blurring or degradations. Simply put, I guess your final classification performance will rely on the input reconstruction result. Unfortunately, the input reconstruction methods will face difficulty when there is a gap between your training and testing datasets.  

Overall, I think this novelty level of concatenating SR/Inpainting inside adversarial training is incremental. The generability of such kind of content reconstruction to real-world data, i.e., making SR works good for a different type of degraded input, is questionable. More importantly, the use case of different kinds of content reconstruction methods is unclear. And I feel this paper is more like a case study since the experimental settings are too narrow to specific data types; thus, the claim is not convincing.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Input recreation is not image inpainting or image super-resolution but defined by the perceptual layer (corruption+recreation+aggregation). Inpainting is not defined for a common input image.

content.title: Input recreation is not image inpainting or image super-resolution but defined by the perceptual layer (corruption+recreation+aggregation). Inpainting is not defined for a common input image.
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for the time in reading and reviewing our paper.

> This paper presents leveraging two input recreation approaches, i.e., inpainting, and super-resolution, to enhance the model robustness against adversarial examples. 

There is a misunderstanding in this statement, since we did not use inpainting or super-resolution to recreate the image. Notice that inpainting is not even defined for an arbitrary input image, since there is no occluded spot for prediction. 

The recreation method uses a perceptual layer with a corruption method, which removes randomly 10% of the image (this is done 10 times and each time a different part is removed), applies inpainting for each of them and then joining them up (effectively recreating the whole image). The resulting single image is feed as output to the DNN. Fig 2 in the original paper illustrates this recreation procedure in detail.

> Why only discuss SR and inpainting, and how do we know what kind of reconstruction approach is the best for a specific type of attack? 

The objective of this paper is not to compare these types of pre-processing but rather to propose a perceptual layer. Notice that creating a perceptual layer needs the design of the tuple mentioned in the paper. If we swap SR with inpainting, for example, it would not work. This happens because inpainting is not defined for an input image as mentioned before and SR is also not defined for occluded images. Each perceptual layer is different and needs to be carefully designed.

>In addition to the choice of content reconstruction, I feel doubtful about your experimental setting. For instance, the training data for image super-resolution obtained by adding noise and bi-linear downsampling is trivial. Doing such ways will bias your reconstruction model to this simple type of degradation. Thus, I am afraid that feeding other types of data will make your model work or not, like different noise distribution or different levels of blurring or degradations. Simply put, I guess your final classification performance will rely on the input reconstruction result. Unfortunately, the input reconstruction methods will face difficulty when there is a gap between your training and testing datasets. 

The learned network is naturally fixed for all the tests. Therefore the gap if any can be spotted in the results. Moreover, to make it even harder for any simple pre-processing systems we included two L\infty and two L0 attacks when evaluating the method. The results show that the method surpasses the state-of-the-art in all datasets and attacks. 

Notice that an important part of using denoising with super-resolution is to make the network rely less on the input itself (resizing it back will make most of the output rely on the predicted input rather than the input itself). The noise is not really related with the type of noise in attacks (as demonstrated by the tests) but rather related with the corruption of the perceptual layer. 

> Overall, I think this novelty level of concatenating SR/Inpainting inside adversarial training is incremental. The generability of such kind of content reconstruction to real-world data, i.e., making SR works good for a different type of degraded input, is questionable. More importantly, the use case of different kinds of content reconstruction methods is unclear. And I feel this paper is more like a case study since the experimental settings are too narrow to specific data types; thus, the claim is not convincing.

Again, we are not concatenating SR/inpainting. Notice that inpainting is not even defined in this case. Moreover, the results are reported for 3 different datasets and 4 types of attacks. This is coherent with tests in other top venues and is anything but a case study.  NSR with adversarial training surpasses the current state-of-the-art in all tests and FIR with adv training surpasses in all but one test which makes the approach arguably strong. In our opinion, the state-of-the-art results and the concept underlying the architecture makes this work very different from an incremental work.

content.title: Feedback to author's comment
content.comment:
Thank you very much for addressing my questions. I leave my thought below.

First, your statement mentions that we did not use inpainting or super-resolution to recreate the image. However, in table 2, isn’t the function phi using inpainting and super-resolution for input recreation?

Secondly, how to generalize your perceptual layer to be capable of defending different types of attack?

Lastly, I am a bit concerned with evaluating optimization-based attacks (i.e., FSFM, PGD, and the proposed method). The proposed adversarial robustness in this paper comes from the combination of random corrupted functions and image recreation. If we consider the $DNN_{\phi} + Classifier$ as the whole system, we can think of it as a “Random Classifier,” where the randomness is encoded in noise addition or random masking. Therefore, following the suggestion in section 4.2&4.3 of the paper – “Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security: Circumventing Defenses to Adversarial Examples,” the attack in the evaluation should consider its differential proxy (such as reparameterization [1, Section 4.3]). I wonder (1) does the author evaluates such type of attack; (2) can gradient update propagate from classifier to the image recreation model in an end2end manner? Otherwise, the attacks used in the experiments are not targeting the whole actual systems.

content.title: Response to reviewer's feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for engaging in the discussion.

> First, your statement mentions that we did not use inpainting or super-resolution to recreate the image. However, in table 2, isn’t the function phi using inpainting and super-resolution for input recreation?

We thought the message mentioned would be clear in the context. Please allow us to rephrase it to "inpainting or super-resolution alone cannot recreate the image as they are not defined for such a task". Perhaps the reviewer is confusing input recreation with the reconstruction of the parts inside each perceptual layer. We want to emphasize that without corruption and aggregation parts, the recreation cannot be achieved.

> Secondly, how to generalize your perceptual layer to be capable of defending different types of attack?

In fact, the method already generalizes to different types of attacks. As mentioned in the rebuttal above, the method is fixed and the tests show how it can take any of the different type of attacks without problems.

> Lastly, I am a bit concerned with evaluating optimization-based attacks (i.e., FSFM, PGD, and the proposed method). The proposed adversarial robustness in this paper comes from the combination of random corrupted functions and image recreation. If we consider the as the whole system, we can think of it as a “Random Classifier,” where the randomness is encoded in noise addition or random masking. Therefore, following the suggestion in section 4.2&4.3 of the paper – “Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security: Circumventing Defenses to Adversarial Examples,” the attack in the evaluation should consider its differential proxy (such as reparameterization [1, Section 4.3]). I wonder (1) does the author evaluates such type of attack; (2) can gradient update propagate from classifier to the image recreation model in an end2end manner? Otherwise, the attacks used in the experiments are not targeting the whole actual systems. 

The worries about attacks which only obfuscate gradients is understandable. However, obfuscated gradients and the problems associated with its lack of security relates to white-box attacks only. 
In the paper "Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security: Circumventing Defenses to Adversarial Examples" it is mentioned that "In this paper, we consider defenses designed for the white-box setting" which is reasonable since many black-box attacks do not need gradients to work.
Our proposed defense is not only a white-box attack defense but a general one and we show it is not merely obfuscating the gradients by showing how black-box attacks fail to work on it. 

In other words, even when attacks do not rely on gradients, its robustness is shown to surpass every defense to date.

By the way, we are not sure what the reviewer mentions as proposed method in " (i.e., FSFM, PGD, and the proposed method).", since we do not propose any attacking method in this paper.

content.title: Update Summary
content.comment:
**-- The reviewers have praised both the idea as well as the results reported in this work. However, giving current borderline scores and even better results in recent tests (added only on the rebuttal phase), we are opting for an withdrawal --**

We would like to thank all reviewers for their time and insightful comments which allowed us to improve the paper further.
In summary, the idea and the results were praised by the reviewers but the experiments and an explanation of the big picture were requested.The article has been updated to reflect the changes inquired by the reviewers.

In summary, the experiment section now uses all samples for PGD and FGSM attacks. This allows for other state-of-the-art defenses to also be included such as LLR and TRADES. We also added a pruned DNN with similar accuracy which reveals that simpler models with lower accuracy have much lower accuracy than current state-of-the-art and the proposed methods (which surpass the state-of-the-art).Moreover, we noticed that a float parameter to the ART library caused the conversion to integer to be rounded to zero, limiting 1px and 10px attacks to only black pixels. This was corrected in the new version which decreased the robustness of defenses, specially FScattering. This made the results even stronger because NSR with adv. training had almost no change in accuracy while FIR with adv. training decreased slightly. We changed the abstract and content to reflect it.

Thus, the results of the paper are even more prominent now. The NSR and FIR with adv. training surpass FScattering in all tests but one in which FIR loses by a mere 0.5% difference. We want to highlight that the accuracy under attack of ϕDNNs are often 2 digits above the state-of-the-art.
